A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LM-assisted NVDRS annotation and codebook-development study. Their text, tables, figures, algorithms, and appendices are readable and can be matched despite the changed title and substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations across 50 variables, expert review of annotation disagreements, simulated codebook development, and a human-in-the-loop legal-interaction case study.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and reports expanded legal-interaction prevalence results and quantified findings from its error analysis.

M1.justification: The annotation and iterative feedback-based codebook algorithms remain substantively unchanged. LM synthesis of guideline updates was already present in v1's Algorithm 1 and Table 8. Explicitly returning the final codebook in v3 formalizes an artifact already generated and evaluated in v1.

E1.justification: The legal-interaction analysis extends NVDRS coverage from 2003–2019 to an expanded collection covering 2003–2023. The domain and tasks remain the same: existing binary variables, simulated codebook development, and three-way legal-interaction classification.

E2.justification: The five-model annotation comparisons, random/coverage sampling comparisons against NVDRS codebooks, and three-model comparisons of initial, expert, and HitL codebooks retain the same comparators. G25 is renamed GHitL and still denotes the codebook selected at iteration 25.

E3.justification: Corpus-wide legal annotation changes from the expert codebook on separate CME/LE collections to the HitL codebook on the expanded pooled collection. Manual development is reported as 150+100+100 narratives, revising v1's description of repeated 150-narrative rounds. The main evaluation sets and 150-case HitL budget remain unchanged; these descriptions do not establish rerunning earlier experiments.

E4.justification: v3 expands the existing mental-health error analysis with quantified failure-mode evidence and adds a FamilyStressor reasoning example. Sampling comparisons and learning-curve analyses are retained, including the relocated HitL curves. Appendix A.1 discusses bootstrap robustness without reporting a new robustness experiment.

E5.justification: v3 adds confidence intervals to the random-set results in Table 4 and the complete 50-variable heatmap. It also corrects textual inter-annotator reliability reporting to Krippendorff's alpha. Existing bootstrap procedures, significance tests, and three temperature-varied runs are retained.

E6.justification: Table 4 changes Qwen2.5-14B agreement from 0.91 to 0.81, below Llama-3-70B's unchanged 0.82. v1's expert-codebook prevalence estimates—15% implicit/0.3% explicit for CME and 10%/0.4% for LE—are replaced by HitL estimates of 12.16%/0.53% on 756,645 narratives. These use different conditions, not a demonstrated performance improvement. v3 also adds 88%/70% failure-mode frequencies and revises reported HitL effort from 3 to 3.5 hours. Main balanced-set and codebook-comparison scores remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs. Coverage calculations and algorithmic stopping computations remain substantively unchanged. The new bootstrap-robustness discussion offers qualitative assumptions and interpretation, not a formal derivation.

C1.justification: The core contributions of annotation validation, inconsistency detection, and expert-assisted codebook development remain. v3 promotes approximately 96K narratives with legal interactions into a headline contribution and clarifies intervention opportunities as motivating deployment of existing prevention approaches in nonclinical settings.

C2.justification: v3 substantially expands applicability qualifications: limited expert validation, a single legal-interaction hypothesis, untested generalization beyond suicide prevention, and absent multi-turn clarification. Appendix B newly interprets selection of model-correct feedback cases, while Appendix A.1 adds assumptions underlying its robustness interpretation. Much of v1's human-oversight and thematic-saturation discussion remains.

D1.justification: v3 newly discloses filtering simulated feedback to model-correct cases, the error-audit sampling and rubric, blinded expert verification, four RTX A6000 GPUs, and detailed annotation roles and timing. It reports code as publicly available rather than forthcoming. Conversely, Table 9 explicitly truncates HitL guidelines printed more fully in v1, reducing documentation of the resulting codebook.

R1.justification: v3 adds clinical-AI reviews and recent NVDRS research, including Chance (2025), Parker (2025), and Wang (2025), and revises comparisons with prior annotation work. The central positioning around expert-assisted codebook refinement and nonclinical intervention opportunities remains; moving related work into the main text is chiefly structural.

P1.justification: v3 retitles the paper and extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, and methodological narrative. It separates setup from analysis, promotes the legal case study and related work to main sections, adds a dedicated Limitations section, and condenses and reorganizes ethics material and appendices.

P2.justification: The paper changes from predominantly single-column to two-column layout. The main heatmap shrinks from 20 to 12 variables, the full heatmap displays confidence intervals, HitL learning curves move to the appendix, and the prevalence chart replaces separate CME/LE series with a pooled series. Tables are extensively reformatted, although some captions retain outdated descriptions.

improvement.justification: v3 improves auditability through detailed error analysis, broader uncertainty reporting, implementation disclosures, and the corrected Table 4 ranking. However, its newly prominent prevalence claim is inconsistently presented: Figure 1 states 10.4% of 270K narratives, Section 4.3 reports 12.7% of 756K, and Figure 7 retains the old dataset caption. Table 9 also truncates previously available guidelines. These gains and losses leave the net quality direction uncertain.
